title: The ghost jobs haunting your job hunt
description:
While job hunting have you ever spotted a job ad that never seems to go away? When you apply you don’t get a reply, let alone a rejection. You may have spotted a ghost! Or a ghost job.

In fact, it’s happening so much ‘ghost jobs’ was on the shortlist for Collins dictionary word of the year (mogging won in the end).

According to a study across the US, UK and Germany up to 22% of jobs posted online last year were listed with no intent to hire. We speak to BBC Business reporter, Megan Lawton about why some companies are choosing to post ‘ghost jobs’ and why some governments are trying to ban them.

Plus, we hear from Sundus who is searching for work and we get some tips from Patricia, a career coach from Nyche careers.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討幽靈職缺現象及其對求職者與勞動力市場的影響。調查顯示線上高達 22% 至 40% 的招募廣告並無實際雇用意圖，企業刊登虛假職缺的目的包括建立人才庫、向競爭對手塑造成長假象，甚至蒐集與販售求職者個人資料。此現象不僅嚴重打擊求職者信心，也會扭曲政府制定政策所需的市場統計數據。目前美國新澤西州、加州與加拿大安大略省正透過立法提高招募透明度，職涯教練 Patricia Parnet 也分享了檢視刊登時間與職物描述等辨識假職缺的警訊。
summaryEn: This episode of What in the World explores the phenomenon of 'ghost jobs'—online job ads posted by employers with no intention to actually hire. BBC business reporter Megan Lawton highlights that between 22% and 40% of online listings may be fake, created by companies to build future talent pools, signal false financial growth to competitors, or harvest applicant data. Beyond demoralizing job seekers, ghost jobs distort official labor statistics used by governments to make economic policies. To tackle this, regions like Ontario in Canada and US states such as New Jersey and California are working on legislation to enforce hiring transparency. Career coach Patricia Parnet also provides practical red flags to help job hunters avoid wasting time on fake listings.
